Response: We appreciate the reviewer highlighting our foundational work on NR2F6. While previous studies have demonstrated the role of NR2F6 as an immune checkpoint, our current study reveals a distinct mechanism. Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells trigger host-mediated epitope spreading in immunocompetent tumor-bearing recipients, thereby inducing antigen-agnostic secondary immune responses.
Our study extends prior work by demonstrating how Nr2f6-modified CAR-T hyperactivity initiates robust immunogenic tumor cell death. This, in turn, catalyzes critical secondary host immune responses. The resulting in situ "self-vaccination" effect establishes polyclonal immune memory against tumor antigens, a mechanism with the potential to overcome major barriers that have historically limited CAR-T efficacy in solid tumors, such as antigenic heterogeneity and antigen downregulation. This process has the potential to deliver durable tumor control, particularly against highly heterogeneous tumors. Furthermore, this process represents a novel therapeutic strategy that eliminates the need for additional interventions, such as lymphodepletion, thereby underscoring its significant translational relevance.
Comment 2) Furthermore, CRISPR is a powerful research tool but there are more specific and novel gene editing techniques.
Response: We acknowledge the emergence of new gene-editing technologies and are exploring their potential for future studies. For this project, we used CRISPR/Cas9, a well-established technology that remains the benchmark for immunotherapy research. A recent review (Hudecek et al. Nat Rev Clin Oncol, 2025, DOI: 10.1038/s41571-025-01072-4), reaffirm the continuing value and feasibility of CRISPR/Cas9 in this field. While we recognize the advances offered by base editors, prime editors, and miniaturized Cas variants, for our proof-of-concept objectives, CRISPR/Cas9 provided the optimal balance of efficacy, robustness, and translational relevance. We are enthusiastic about novel developments and are actively exploring their potential for future studies.
Comment 3) The authors also use a single tumor model (no general applicability demonstrated in other tumor) and an antigen (Epcam) that is expressed in healthy epithelial cells.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that demonstrating efficacy in additional tumor models is essential to strengthening the generalizability of our findings. Accordingly, we expanded our analysis to include two independent in vivo models using B16-F10 melanoma and MC38 colon cancer cell lines that were engineered to express human EGFR (NEW Supplementary Figures 2A–G). In both syngeneic settings, Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T therapy achieved superior tumor control and improved survival. This confirms that its applicability extends beyond the initial Panc02-EpCAM model. These data demonstrate that our approach is not restricted to a single tumor type or antigen.
Manuscript addition (lines 217-223): "To demonstrate broader applicability, we employed two independent CAR-T mouse models expressing an anti-human EGFR 28ζ CAR, together with syngeneic B16-F10 and MC38 tumor cells transduced with human EGFR (hereafter referred to as B16-F10-hEGFR and MC38-hEGFR). In both additional models, Nr2f6-depleted CAR-T-treated animals exhibited superior tumor control and prolonged survival compared with NTC CAR-T recipients (Suppl.Fig2A–G). These findings underline the broader relevance of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells, which achieve more effective and durable tumor clearance across distinct solid-tumor models.”
Regarding EpCAM expression in healthy epithelial cells: Previous preclinical and clinical studies have reported limited off-tumor toxicity for EpCAM-directed CAR-T therapies, with ongoing clinical trials confirming tolerable safety and encouraging efficacy profiles (PMID: 32923168; DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adg9721; NCT02915445).
Comment 4) The challenges of targeting specific antigens on the tumor cell surface and heterogeneity of expression, which are the major limitations in the field, are not addressed at all in this study.
Response: To model clinically relevant tumor antigen heterogeneity, we used Panc02 tumor cells that were approximately 70% EpCAM-positive. This created a stringent setting to assess both direct and indirect anti-EpCAM CAR-T effects. Using this approach, we were able to demonstrate epitope spreading and host immune involvement in controlling EpCAM antigen-negative tumor variants. We have revised the Methods and Results sections to clarify our rationale for selecting heterogeneous target cells, and confirm that this information now appears explicitly in the manuscript.
Manuscript addition (lines 202-205): “To assess anti-tumor efficacy of non-targeting control (NTC) and Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T, we inoculated immunocompetent mice with Panc02-EpCAM tumor cells comprising approximately 70% antigen-positive cells to introduce tumor heterogeneity and model clinically relevant challenges.”
Comment 5) On the other hand, the demonstration of a boost in polyclonal pre-existing, endogenous T cell responses, while not unexpected or blatantly novel (previous studies have shown that for other CAR-T cells), is interesting nevertheless.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the significance of the secondary, polyclonal, host anti-tumor immune memory response that extends immunity well beyond the initial CAR target. Previous studies have shown that combining vaccination with CAR-T therapy can enhance endogenous T cell responses (Ma et al., Cell, 2023, DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2023.06.002). Additionally, recent publications from 2025 underscore a rapidly growing consensus that driving secondary, host-mediated, antigen-agnostic immune control is a critical frontier for advancing CAR-T therapy against heterogeneous solid tumors, thereby directly validating our mechanistic strategy. For instance, armored CAR-T cells engineered to express cytokines such as IL-7, CCL19, IL-12, or IL-18 have demonstrated enhanced recruitment and activation of dendritic cells and endogenous T cells, promoting epitope spreading (Mohamed et al., JITC, 2025, DOI: 10.1136/jitc-2024-00999; Li et al., J Immunother Cancer, 2025, DOI: 10.1136/jitc-2024-010581). Similarly, chemokine-secreting CAR-T cells, such as XCL1, have been shown to recruit cDC1s and boost endogenous CD8+ T cell responses (Li et al., J Immunother Cancer, 2025, DOI: 10.1136/jitc-2024-010581).
In a distinct and unprecedented advance over these multi-component engineering approaches, our study is the first to show that targeted NR2F6 gene editing in CAR-T cells alone; without additional cytokine expression, vaccination, or combinatorial manipulations, is sufficient to robustly and reproducibly drive broad, polyclonal host immunity and effective immune control of antigenically diverse solid tumors in vivo. This streamlined, single-gene editing strategy not only establishes a new mechanism, distinct from current approaches, but also highlights an innovative and clinically actionable path toward next-generation CAR-T therapies with enhanced efficacy for solid tumor treatment.
OTHER MAJOR COMMENTS
Comment 6) -The phenotypes (e.g., GZMs, TCF1) shown in vitro in Figures 2-4 need to be shown in vivo in TILs. The problem is that CAR-T cells do not persist in vivo at day 13, edited or not, which is a major concern.
Response: We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding CAR-T cell persistence in vivo. While it is true that CAR-T cells in our model do not persist beyond day 13, this limited persistence is not necessarily detrimental. Rather, the transient presence of highly functional Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T cells effectively prime and empower the endogenous immune system, leading to a durable, polyclonal anti-tumor response. Such a mechanism of CAR-T-induced activation of endogenous host immunity has been increasingly recognized as a key route to achieve long-term tumor control despite limited CAR-T persistence (von G López-Cantillo et al. , Front. Immun., 2022; DOI: 10.3389/fimmu.2022.878209; Guerra et al., Int. J. Mol. Sci., 2021, DOI: 10.3390/ijms23010405).
To substantiate our findings, we now include in vivo phenotyping data (NEW Fig. 1F–J, day 3 post-therapy) demonstrating enhanced CAR-T infiltration into tumors, elevated TCF-1 expression in tumor-draining lymph nodes, and increased IFNγ and granzyme B production upon ex vivo restimulation. These observations confirm that Nr2f6-depleted CAR-T cells exhibit early, functionally potent effector and memory-linked phenotypes that initiate a host-driven immune cascade resulting in sustained tumor control. The results demonstrate that Nr2f6-depleted CAR-T cells exert early, potent effector-linked functions in vivo, which are linked to the initiation of a host-driven immune cascade that establishes sustained tumor control, even in the absence of long-term CAR-T cell persistence.
Manuscript addition (lines 227–236): “On day 3 after adoptive CAR-T cell transfer (ACT), we observed an increased fraction of Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells within the tumor compared to NTC-treated controls (Fig1F). Notably, flow cytometry analysis revealed that Nr2f6-depleted CAR-T cells in the tumor-draining lymph node (tdLN) express elevated levels of TCF1 protein (Fig1G, H), a key transcription factor shown to regulate T cell memory formation and stemness (Escobar et al., 2020, Utzschneider et al., 2016). To assess their cytotoxic phenotype, we re-stimulated NTC and Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells from spleens of tumor-bearing mice ex vivo with target tumor cells. Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells produced significantly higher amounts of interferon gamma (IFNγ) and granzyme B (GrzB) compared to controls (Fig1I, J), supporting their enhanced effector function.””
Comment 7) This reviewer could not figure out the origin of the scFv used to re-direct CAR-T cells against Epcam, but it is likely that it could be recognized as ‘foreign” in immunocompetent mice.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. The scFv used to redirect CAR-T cells against EpCAM originates from the rat anti-EpCAM monoclonal antibody clone G8.8 (IgG2a). As expected from its non-murine origin, this scFv is immunogenic in immunocompetent mice and likely contributes to the limited persistence of CAR-T cells observed in our model. Importantly, rather than impairing therapeutic outcome, this transient CAR-T presence was sufficient to induce potent tumor rejection, underscoring the capacity of Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells to trigger host-mediated immune amplification. The observed tumor control despite immunogenic CAR-T depletion firmly supports our proposed mechanism, in which NR2F6 editing promotes cross-priming and the establishment of durable, antigen-agnostic endogenous immunity.
Manuscript addition (lines 191-193): “This 28ζ CAR comprises an scFv fragment derived from the rat anti-EpCAM antibody clone G8.8, fused to intracellular CD28 and CD3ζ signaling domains connected via a CD8 hinge and CD28 transmembrane region (Fig. 1A).”
Comment 8) -Toxicity and on target, off-tumor effects are important concerns that are not addressed
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding potential toxicity and on-target, off-tumor effects. Despite the known lung accumulation of EpCAM-targeted CAR-T cells, we observed no overt signs of toxicity, weight loss, or distress throughout the study (NEW Supplementary Fig. 1A–C). We attribute this favorable safety profile to two key factors: (i) the comparatively low CAR-T cell dose administered (3.6 × 10⁶ cells), which is below standard preclinical dosing regimens, and (ii) the omission of lymphodepletion, thereby minimizing systemic cytokine release and collateral tissue effects.
Consistent with our findings, previous preclinical and clinical studies have reported limited off-tumor toxicity for EpCAM-directed CAR-T therapies, with ongoing clinical trials confirming tolerable safety and encouraging efficacy profiles (PMID: 32923168; DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adg9721; NCT02915445).
Collectively, these data support the translational feasibility of EpCAM-based CAR-T strategies when applied under controlled dosing conditions, such as ours. Importantly, the absence of any pathological or clinical toxicity in our Nr2f6-edited CAR-T treated groups further underscores that the enhanced antitumor efficacy observed is not accompanied by increased on-target, off-tumor activity, highlighting a distinctly favorable therapeutic index.
Manuscript addition (lines 536–538): “Importantly, we observed no toxicity or on-target/off-tumor effects, underscoring that the use of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells without lymphodepletion represents a promising strategy with minimal adverse effects while preserving potent endogenous antitumor immunity.”
Reviewer #2:
The authors are investigating the role of transcription factor NR2F6, recently identified as T cell checkpoint, in antigen spreading (AS) in the context of CAR-T cell therapy. They employ NR2F6 KO to address their thesis.
Comment 1) The more common term for AS is epitope spreading, defined as diversification of epitope specificity, and it typically requires cross-presentation of extracellular antigens in MHC-I context (https://doi.org/10.1038/nri724; https://doi.org/10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-20-0305).
Response: Thank you for this correction. We have replaced 'antigen spreading' with 'epitope spreading' throughout the manuscript to reflect established terminology.
Comment 2) The manuscript is well written, and experimental results are compelling. However, some results are in my opinion overstated/overinterpreted. You focus on AS as the main MOA (mechanism of action) of the NR2F6 KO in T cells rejecting tumors in vivo, but the experimental proof of AS being primarily responsible for the observed anti-tumor effect needs to be stronger for such statements.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our study and for raising this important point regarding the mechanistic interpretation of epitope spreading (ES). While alternative mechanisms may also contribute, multiple lines of complementary in vivo and ex vivo evidence now support ES as a key driver of tumor rejection mediated by Nr2f6-deficient T cells. Specifically, we observe the following:
(i) an increased proportion of host tumor-associated antigen-specific effector CD3⁺ T cells by ELISPOT (see previous Fig.5H–I);
(ii) elevated frequencies of cross-presenting cDC1 cells and corresponding innate activation signatures in TILs and spleens (see previous Fig.5D–E);
(iii) robust rejection of EpCAM-negative Panc02 tumors upon rechallenge, indicative of epitope spreading (see previous Fig.6A–C); and
(iv) adoptive transfer of primed splenocytes conferring tumor control independently of residual CAR-T cells (see previous Fig.6A–E). In addition, single-cell TCR sequencing revealed increased TCR diversity and reduced clonality in tumors from complete responders (see previous Fig.7E). Finally, our new early in vivo phenotyping data (day 3 post-therapy; NEW Fig.1F–J, NEW Supplementary Fig.3A-G) demonstrate enhanced endogenous activation, which is consistent with the initiation of host immunity.
Taken together, these complementary datasets provide robust evidence in support of ES as a key mechanism of tumor rejection in this model, without ruling out the possibility of additional contributions from other Nr2f6-associated functional effects. We have revised the text to ensure that the mechanistic interpretation remains balanced and consistent with the data presented.
Please also see our detailed response to your Comment 11 below.
Comment 3) It would be nice to see direct data on broadening of Panc.02-relevant T cell repertoire in mice after vs before CAR therapy with NR2F6 KO cells to strengthen your main hypothesis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. While a comprehensive pre- and post-therapy TCR repertoire analysis was beyond the present study’s technical reach, we did analyse TCR diversity in TILs from our memory/rechallenge experiments, which revealed an increase in TCR diversity among Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T treated animals (see Fig.7E). Recent CAR T cell studies (Cheloni et al., Nat Comm, 2025) demonstrate that endogenous TCR repertoire changes are generally not observed early after CAR T cell therapy; substantial alterations within the host T cell pool (including repertoire broadening, increased diversity, and enrichment of tumor-relevant clonotypes) typically emerge only at later time points, particularly in long-term memory or rechallenge settings. Consistent with this, our memory/rechallenge experiments revealed a marked increase in TCR diversity among Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T treated animals (see Fig. 7E). Focused analyses of high-frequency tumor-reactive clones in blood samples did not show pronounced compositional shifts 12 days after therapy, supporting published work indicating that early endogenous TCR repertoire remains largely unchanged. Notably, enrichment of CD3⁺ T cells following Nr2f6-edited CAR-T therapy (Reviewer Fig. 1) supports the enhancement of endogenous immunity over time.
Together, these results, in line with recent reports, underscore that endogenous TCR repertoire broadening and adaptation are mainly manifest during the memory phase following CAR T therapy, and not in the immediate effector phase.
Reviewer Figure 1 Analysis of T cell abundance and TCR repertoire in blood pre- and post-CAR-T therapy. (A) CD3⁺ T cell frequencies among lymphocytes before therapy (white), after non-targeting control CAR-T (gray), and after Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T (green), with individual mouse data and statistical comparison. (B–C) Dominant TCR Vβ family usage among CD8⁺ (B) and CD4⁺ (C) T cells pre- and post-therapy (12 days after CAR-T transfer) for both groups. Color legend denotes TCR Vβ segments; gray indicates undefined clones. Data show no major changes in dominant TCR clones post-therapy, but increased CD3⁺ T cell frequencies in the Nr2f6-edited group, supporting enhanced endogenous T cell responses.
Comment 4) Can you rule out other mechanisms, such as heightened anti-tumor reactivity, increased viability, proliferation, metabolic fitness, increased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFNg) or lower exhaustion of KO effector T cells vs AS, or other?
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting the importance of defining the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor activity of Nr2f6-deficient T cells. Previous work, including from our group, has established NR2F6 as an intracellular immune checkpoint that limits T cell effector function, cytokine production (IFNγ, IL-2, TNFα), viability, and metabolic activity, while promoting exhaustion (Klepsch et al., Nat Commun, 2018; Jakic et al., Cell Death Dis, 2021; H. Miftah et al., Front Immunol, 2023). These well-characterised cell-intrinsic effects explain the heightened anti-tumor reactivity of Nr2f6-deficient conventional T cells.
In the current work, we extend these mechanisms to CAR-T cells and uncover additional, previously underexplored features, including improved metabolic fitness, reduced exhaustion, and robust early effector cytokine production within the solid tumor microenvironment. Most importantly, our in vivo data now demonstrate that these hyper-reactive Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells can efficiently prime endogenous immunity, triggering durable, polyclonal host responses through epitope spreading (NEW Fig.1F-J, previous Fig.5D-H, Fig.6A-E, Fig.7E, NEW Supplementary Fig.3A-H). Thus, while superior intrinsic viability and cytokine output clearly contribute to improved direct cytotoxicity, our findings reveal a distinct and functionally separable mechanism: Nr2f6-modified, metabolically fit CAR-T cells serve as in situ immune catalysts that amplify secondary host anti-tumor responses through effective cross-priming. This represents a conceptual advance beyond earlier studies and supports Nr2f6 inhibition as a dual-acting strategy, enhancing both CAR-T cell potency and the endogenous immune response to achieve more durable tumor control.
Comment 5) Is the AS benefit mediated only by the modified (NR2F6 KO and CART+) CD8T cells, or is it also perpetrated by non-modified autologous T cells in the mice? This may shed light on the MOA.
Response: Our data suggest that the epitope spreading benefit requires modified Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T cells, since CAR transgene un-transduced T cells did not have any effect (see previous Supplementary Figure 1 / NEW Supplementary Figure 4C). Although endogenous T cells contribute to sustained downstream responses, the CAR-modified population is essential for initiating this cascade.
Major comments/Abstract and Introduction.
Comment 6) You speak of treatment of solid tumors in general, but only employ one model of pancreatic cancer: e Panc02 tumors. Please qualify your statements accordingly to your scope of work.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. As addressed in our response to Reviewer 1, Comment 3, we have extended our experimental scope beyond the Panc02 pancreatic cancer model to additionally include two independent solid tumor models—B16-F10-hEGFR melanoma and MC38-hEGFR colon carcinoma (see NEW Supplementary Fig. 2A–G). These models were deliberately chosen because they represent immunologically distinct tumor microenvironments: B16-F10 melanomas are poorly immunogenic with low T cell infiltration, whereas MC38 colon tumors are comparatively immune-responsive.
The demonstration of consistent Nr2f6-deleted CAR-T efficacy across these diverse systems confirms the broader applicability of our findings and strengthens the translational relevance of the mechanism described. We have also qualified manuscript statements accordingly to reflect this expanded scope.
Manuscript addition (lines 217-223): “To demonstrate broader applicability, we employed two independent CAR-T mouse models expressing an anti-human EGFR 28ζ CAR, together with syngeneic B16-F10 and MC38 tumor cells transduced with human EGFR (hereafter referred to as B16-F10-hEGFR and MC38-hEGFR). In both additional models, Nr2f6-depleted CAR-T-treated animals exhibited superior tumor control and prolonged survival compared with NTC CAR-T recipients (Suppl.Fig2A–G). These findings underline the broader relevance of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells, which achieve more effective and durable tumor clearance across distinct solid-tumor models.”
Comment 7) Please define your hypothesis more precisely: (e.g. KO of NR2F6 promotes AS in the context of CAR-T cell therapy? Or promotes other/additional effects..), and include a corresponding sentence in the abstract and intro.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion to refine and explicitly define our working hypothesis. As requested, we have clarified the conceptual framework in both the Abstract and Introduction of the revised manuscript. Our hypothesis is that Nr2f6 deletion enhances the intrinsic activation state and effector function of CAR-T cells, which in turn promotes a secondary, endogenous anti-tumor immune response through antigen-agnostic epitope spreading. This is consistent with recent findings highlighting that targeting NR2F6 or its signalling pathway can potentiate CAR-T efficacy by inducing immunogenic tumor cell death and promoting systemic epitope spreading. This dual mechanism integrates the direct, cytotoxic effects of Nr2f6-edited CAR-T cells with their ability to prime endogenous host immunity.
Manuscript additions: Abstract (lines 60-61): “We postulate that the intrinsic benefits of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells enhance anti-tumor immunity by promoting secondary endogenous responses through epitope spreading.”
Introduction (lines 161–163): “We therefore hypothesized that deletion of Nr2f6 could reprogram CAR-T cells toward a metabolically fitter, less exhausted state, capable of initiating robust adaptive immune amplification through tumor antigen cross priming and epitope spreading.”
Comment 8) Reference to relevant literature: NR2F6 appears to play a role both in cancer cells (e.g. AML, glioma, lung cancer, melanoma…) and in immune (T ) cells. To provide a balanced intro, please briefly allude also to the role of this factor in tumor cells, vs the immune compartment. A recent report described both tumor intrinsic and tumor-extrinsic benefits of NR2F6 down-modulation in the context of immunotherapy of melanoma tumors DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adf6621. How does your current work differentiate itself and add to the existing knowledge on this subject? Please add in intro or discussion vs this or similar recent references.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment and have expanded both the Introduction and Discussion to provide a balanced perspective on NR2F6’s dual functions in cancer biology. Recent work has established that NR2F6 exerts both tumor-intrinsic and immune-extrinsic effects. In melanoma, tumor cell-intrinsic NR2F6 represses interferon-γ–regulated genes and immune-stimulatory pathways, enabling immune evasion, whereas Nr2f6 loss sensitizes tumors to PD-1 blockade (H. Kim et al., Sci. Adv., 2023; DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adf6621). These findings complement earlier reports identifying NR2F6 as a T cell-intrinsic immune checkpoint controlling NFAT/AP-1–dependent cytokine transcription and effector function (Klepsch et al. Nat. Commun., 2018, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-04004-2). Building on these discoveries, our present study focuses exclusively on the immune cell-intrinsic axis of NR2F6 regulation in engineered CAR-T cells. In contrast to tumor-intrinsic Nr2f6 inhibition, our work demonstrates that targeted deletion of Nr2f6 in CAR-T cells alone is sufficient to enhance early effector function and—critically—to initiate epitope spreading-driven endogenous immunity in solid tumors. This approach provides a complementary and translationally distinct framework for immunotherapeutic NR2F6 targeting.
Manuscript addition (Introduction, lines 156-158): “Moreover, NR2F6 expression in melanoma cells contributes to immune evasion and tumor progression, underscoring its dual role in the tumor microenvironment (Kim et al., 2023).”
Results:
Comment 9) In your experimental design, did you modify only CD8 T cells, or all T cells with NR2F6 KO and CAR- ? please clarify.
Response: We used CD8+ T cells exclusively for Nr2f6 knockout and CAR transduction in the experiments reported. During revision, we included limited CD4+ CAR-T data (see NEW Supplementary Figure 2H–K) in response to questions from you (comment 10 + 16) and Reviewer 3 (comment 2).
Comment 10) Page 4:” We did not observe any differences in CAR transduction efficiency (Fig2A) or expansion of Nr2f6-/- or wild type CD8+ T cells during CAR-T cell production (Suppl.Fig2B).” Did you look at CD4 T cells? Do they contribute to the beneficial effects you observed in vitro or in vivo? Please report.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question regarding the role of CD4+ T cells. While the original manuscript did not address CD4+ T cells, prompted by reviewer feedback, we analysed CD4+ CAR-T cells. Our data show that CD4+ CAR-T cells do not enhance the beneficial tumor phenotype mediated by CD8+ CAR-T cells (see NEW Supplementary Figure 2H–K). This may reflect the transient presence of CAR-T cells in our model, where the effects of long-term CD4+ support cannot be observed.
Manuscript addition (lines 240-245): “Of note, and focusing on CAR persistence, some reports highlight the crucial role of CD4+ T cells promoting and sustaining CAR-T cell responses in long term responders (Melenhorst et al., 2022). We transferred a mixture of CD8+ and CD4+ Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells to evaluate the impact of CD4 help, but could not observe a beneficial effect on tumor growth comparing to CD8 only therapy (Suppl.Fig2H-K).'
Comment 11) Page 7:” Therefore, the observed immune defense against the tumor after the apparent disappearance of CAR-T cells can be well explained by AS and the subsequent induction of a strong secondary tumor antigen-specific T cell response. Overall, we demonstrate a cooperative anti-tumor effect of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T therapy and endogenous immune cells.” You purport AS, but present little direct data of AS in vivo or ex vivo… Were cDC1 you identified involved in prolongation of anti-tumor responses after T cells were gone? Were other cells recruited? What was their phenotype?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this crucial question and the opportunity to clarify our interpretation of epitope spreading (ES) as one principal mechanism in our model. Recognizing the inherent complexity of demonstrating ES directly in vivo, we employed multiple complementary in vivo and ex vivo approaches aligned with established definitions of ES in cancer immunotherapy—the expansion and diversification of endogenous T cell responses to secondary tumor antigens beyond the initial CAR target, coordinated primarily by antigen-presenting cells such as cDC1s, and associated with durable anti-tumor immunity.
Our principal findings include:
• Increased tumor-associated antigen-specific CD3⁺ T cells by ELISPOT after CAR-T therapy, using re-stimulation with Panc02 peptide-pulsed dendritic cells, tumor lysate, or cell line antigens (previous Fig5.G, H).
• Elevated frequencies of cDC1 cross-presenting dendritic cells in TILs and spleens, providing essential cross-priming for CD8⁺ T cell activation (previous Fig.5E, F).
• Rejection of EpCAM-negative Panc02 tumors upon rechallenge in complete responder mice, functionally demonstrating control of antigen-loss variants, a hallmark of productive ES (previous Fig.6 A-C).
• Adoptive transfer of splenocytes from complete responders conferring tumor control in naïve mice, independent of CAR-T cells, with high IFNγ recall responses ex vivo, indicating induction of durable, host-mediated memory (previous Fig.6D, - E).
• Single-cell TCR sequencing showing increased diversity and reduced clonality in TILs from responders, consistent with repertoire broadening triggered by CAR-T-induced immunogenic tumor cell death (previous Fig.7E).
• Early post-therapy phenotyping (day 3) revealing enhanced activation of endogenous CD8⁺ Tpex cells (NEW Supplementary Fig.3A-E), increased CD8-IFNg+ producing cells (NEW Supplementary Fig.3F), and elevated NK cell numbers in tumor-draining lymph nodes (NEW Supplementary Fig.3G), supporting elimination of antigen-negative targets.
• Regarding other immune cell recruitment, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed increased populations of proliferating CD8+ T cells, Th2 cells, macrophages, and cDC1s in treated animals (previous Fig.7B, D).
While alternative mechanisms may also contribute, multiple lines of complementary in vivo and ex vivo evidence now align with a mechanistic model in which ES acts as a central determinant of durable tumor control. Our data show that Nr2f6-deleted CAR-T cells synergize with endogenous antigen-presenting and effector cell networks to broaden the antitumor immune repertoire, sustain tumor rejection beyond CAR-T cell persistence, and limit antigenic escape. We have revised the manuscript to clarify this cooperative interplay between Nr2f6-edited CAR-T cells, epitope spreading, and both adaptive and innate immune recruitment as the integrated mechanistic forces that drive durable and diversified antitumor immunity in our model.
Comment 12) “Therefore, the observed immune defense against the tumor after the apparent disappearance of CAR-T cells can be well explained by AS and the subsequent induction of a strong secondary tumor antigen-specific T cell response. Overall, we demonstrate a cooperative anti-tumor effect of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T therapy and endogenous immune cells.” – please consider revising this statement to match the strength of your data. If I understood correctly, you only showed the ability of cDC to generate enhanced T cell priming of NR2F6 KO CD8 T cells in vitro, but not proven that this happened during your in vivo experiment and was indeed responsible for accelerated tumor clearance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important feedback and fully agree that direct in vivo proof of secondary antigen-specific T cell induction and the exclusive role of cDC1s remains correlative in our current study. In line with your suggestion, we have revised the statement in the text to accurately reflect the strength and scope of our data.
Our evidence supporting ES as a principal mechanism relies on a robust combination of complementary in vivo and ex vivo readouts:
• Elevated cDC1 levels in tumors and spleens, together with increased IL-12p40, supporting increased cross-presentation capacity and a pro-inflammatory microenvironment (previous Fig.5E-F).
• Adoptive transfer experiments, where splenocytes from complete responders provided antigen-independent tumor control—strongly indicative of durable endogenous immunity (previous Fig.6D).
• Early and sustained phenotypic recruitment of endogenous adaptive and innate immune populations (CD8+, Th2, cDC1s, NK, macrophages) by flow cytometry and single-cell sequencing (previous Fig. 5E, previous Fig.7A-D, NEW Supplementary Figure 3 A-G).
We acknowledge that, due to the phenotypic diversity of antigen-presenting cells within the tumor microenvironment, it is plausible that other APC subsets, such as monocyte-derived DCs, macrophages, or B cells, also contribute to amplifying endogenous T cell responses in this setting. Although we did not find a definitive phenotypic change in these cell types in our current datasets, this possibility is explicitly discussed as a potential avenue for follow-up mechanistic studies:
Manuscript addition (lines 554-557): “While our data highlight the critical role of cDC1s in this process, we do not exclude potential contributions from other antigen-presenting cell populations, such as monocyte-derived dendritic cells, macrophages, or B cells, which warrant further investigation in future studies.
Comment 13) “The data support the concept that NR2F6-modified CAR-T therapy apparently facilitates the occurrence of AS, which results in a robust secondary polyclonal immune response induced by the crosstalk of endogenous innate and adaptive immune cell compartments.”
- Again, please prove that a robust secondary polyclonal immune response occurred in vivo, or rephrase.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment and have carefully revised our manuscript statements to reflect the scope and strength of our in vivo evidence for a robust, secondary polyclonal immune response. In our model, mice treated with Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells not only completely rejected antigen-positive Panc02 tumors, but also exhibited tumor rejection upon rechallenge with antigen-negative variants (previous Fig.6A–C), at a time point when CAR-T cells were no longer detectable. This functional rejection of antigen-loss variants, which lack the CAR target, provides strong evidence for durable, CAR-independent endogenous tumor immunity—a phenomenon widely accepted as a hallmark of productive epitope spreading and polyclonal T cell response activation.
Complementing these rechallenge data, TCR repertoire sequencing in complete responder mice revealed decreased clonality and increased TCR diversity (previous Fig.7E), strongly supporting expansion and diversification of the host T cell repertoire consistent with polyclonal immunity. While these findings collectively provide compelling evidence for a broad, secondary endogenous T cell response, we fully acknowledge that the precise cellular and antigenic determinants require further delineation and have moderated our interpretations accordingly throughout the text.
Manuscript addition (Conclusion on p19, lines 570-576):This study identifies NR2F6 as a T-cell-intrinsic metabolic checkpoint that limits CAR-T cell function in solid tumors. Deletion of Nr2f6 enhances exhaustion resilience and sustains antitumor activity by coupling cytotoxic reinvigoration with dendritic cell-dependent cross-priming and epitope spreading (ES). These preclinical findings provide a rationale for targeting NR2F6 to overcome immunosuppression and antigenic heterogeneity in solid tumors, with potential relevance for improving CAR-T and other cell-based immunotherapies in human cancer.”
Comment 14) Figure 8 is very general and doesn’t point out the specific MOA through which NR2F6 KO benefits CAR-T cell therapy in your proposed model. Please revise.
Response: We have comprehensively revised Figure 8 to highlight the mechanistic pathways through which Nr2f6 knockout enhances CAR-T therapy, including improved cytotoxicity, epitope spreading and endogenous memory formation.
Graphical Summary in Figure 8: Functional advantages and mechanisms underlying Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cell therapy in a solid tumor model: A. In vitro: Conventional CAR-T cells exhibit reduced cytotoxicity, impaired cytokine release, increased exhaustion, and diminished metabolic fitness. In contrast, Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells display enhanced tumor-cell killing, increased IFNγ production, and improved metabolic performance under repetitive stimulation. B. In vivo: Schematic depiction of therapeutic dynamics following CAR-T cell infusion into solid tumor-bearing mice. Conventional CAR-T cells progressively lose efficacy due to antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive cues within the tumor microenvironment (TME), and cumulative dysfunction. In comparison, Nr2f6-modified CAR-T therapy induces immunogenic tumor cell death, facilitates antigen uptake and presentation by host antigen-presenting cells (APCs), and immune responses beyond the initial CAR target. C. Overall concept: The major limitations of conventional CAR-T cells in solid tumors, antigen heterogeneity, a suppressive TME, and limited persistence, are overcome by Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells. These cells retain sustained cytotoxic activity, effectively target heterogeneous tumor antigens, and provoke a durable, polyclonal host immune memory response. For the first time, this approach demonstrates that antigenically diverse solid tumors can be efficiently eradicated, bridging the efficacy gap between hematologic and solid malignancies in CAR-T therapy. All schematics are conceptual representations summarizing the cellular and molecular events that collectively underlie the enhanced therapeutic efficacy of Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells.
Discussion:
Comment 15) Are your findings regarding NF2F6 function in cancer immunotherapy confined to the specific mouse-strand you used, or can they be generalized, why? How broadly can they be generalized to mouse experimental systems? To human health? Please speculate or provide data/refs to support your points.
Response: Thank you for raising this important question regarding the generalizability of our NR2F6 findings in cancer immunotherapy. We have expanded the Discussion to clarify that NR2F6 exhibits a high degree of homology and functional conservation between mouse and human, supporting the broader relevance of our data. Previous work from our group and others (Klepsch et al., Nat. Commun., 2018; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-04004-2; Hermann-Kleiter et al., Cell Rep., 2015, DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.035) has demonstrated that NR2F6 ablation leads to augmented effector function and hyper-reactivity in both mouse and human T cells, underscoring its conserved immunoregulatory role. Notably, Nr2f6-deficient mice consistently display enhanced tumor control and effector responses across distinct genetic backgrounds, indicating that these effects are not limited by mouse strain.
Clinical relevance is supported by recent human melanoma studies that correlate NR2F6 expression with impaired anti-tumor immunity and show that its targeting can restore effector function and responsiveness to immunotherapy (Kim et al., Sci Adv, 2023; DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adf6621). Collectively, these data argue that the anti-tumor effects of Nr2f6 deletion identified in our study reflect a broadly conserved mechanism not restricted to a single mouse strain and provide compelling support for translational application in human cancer immunotherapy. These points have been clarified with new references in the revised Discussion.
Comment 16) What happens with CD4 T cells in your models? Is NR2F6 important for CD4 T cells?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. NR2F6 plays a well-established immunoregulatory role in CD4⁺ T cells, particularly in modulating helper T cell differentiation and cytokine expression. Previous studies have shown that NR2F6 functions as a transcriptional repressor of NFAT:AP-1-dependent genes and limits the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, IL-17, and IFNγ, thereby restraining Th17 differentiation and effector CD4 responses (Hermann-Kleiter et al., Cell Rep, 2015; DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2015.08.035; Klepsch et al., Nat Commun, 2018. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-04004-2; Klepsch et al., Cell Commun Signal, 2021, DOI: 10.1186/s12964-019-0454-z). Mechanistically, NR2F6 directly interferes with NFAT:AP-1 DNA binding and acts as a PKC-regulated transcriptional checkpoint, maintaining appropriate activation thresholds in CD4⁺ T cells.
However, our new experiments show that, within our CAR-T context, CD4⁺ CAR-T cells do not significantly contribute to the enhanced tumor-rejection phenotype mediated by Nr2f6-deficient CD8⁺ CAR-T cells (see NEW Supplementary Fig.2H–K). These data indicate that, while NR2F6 remains functionally important in CD4 T cell biology, its contribution to the observed therapeutic effects in this specific CAR-T setting appears secondary to that of CD8⁺ effector cells. We have clarified this distinction in the manuscript to reflect the cell-type specificity of NR2F6 function.
Manuscript addition (discussion, lines 516-518): NR2F6 exerts immunoregulatory control in both CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells, but our data indicate that the enhanced antitumor activity is primarily mediated by CD8⁺ CAR-T cells (Suppl.Fig2H–K).”
Comment 17) Does AS in your model systems occur only via the modified KO T cells, CAR+ T cells, both modifications only, or also is carried out by “naïve”, non-modified host’s T cells?
Response: Thank you for highlighting this mechanistic point. Our experiments demonstrate that the augmented epitope spreading and polyclonal, endogenous immune response in our models requires the presence of Nr2f6-knockout CAR-T cells. This effect is not observed with Nr2f6-depleted un-transduced, non-CAR-T cells (see NEW Supplementary Fig.4C / OLD Suppl.Fig.1). These findings indicate that only the combination of CAR expression and Nr2f6 inhibition in T cells enables sufficient tumor cell killing and antigen release to potentiate secondary, host-mediated immune priming and robust epitope spreading. While we cannot fully exclude limited activation of endogenous host T cells, our data show that the observed durability of the anti-tumor response is not generated by naïve or non-modified T cells alone. Instead, the combinatorial effect of Nr2f6-knockout together with CAR modification is required to initiate the cross-priming and expansion of secondary tumor-antigen–specific T cell clones seen in our model.
Manuscript addition (Discussion, lines 518–522): “ The observed ES effect likewise depends mainly on Nr2f6-modified CAR-T cells, as untransduced bystander T cells failed to confer this benefit (Suppl.Fig4C). Still, we cannot fully exclude minor supportive contributions from endogenous, non-modified T cells that may be secondarily activated following CAR-T-mediated tumor recognition.””
Comment 18) Does AS work via cytokine secretion, boosting the activity of cDCs, or decreasing activation threshold in T cells (modified or not), or other mechanisms? Please propose specific and detailed mechanisms as you see fit and describe in the discussion.
Response: We appreciate this mechanistic question. Based on our results and supported by current literature, we propose that epitope spreading in our model is driven by Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells through three main mechanisms: (1) enhanced cytokine secretion (e.g., IFNγ, that boosts dendritic cell activity and cross-priming); (2) a reduced T cell exhaustion threshold, enabling stronger and faster CAR-T function; and (3) subsequent recruitment and activation of endogenous innate and adaptive immune cells. These effects jointly facilitate immunogenic tumor cell death, dendritic cell activation, and broadening of the host T cell repertoire—a process known to underlie durable, polyclonal antitumor responses in CAR-T therapy.
Manuscript addition (lines 557-562): “ Mechanistically, epitope spreading is likely orchestrated through multiple complementary pathways: enhanced IFNγ secretion by Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells amplifies cDC1 activation; loss of NR2F6 lowers the activation threshold of CAR-T cells, inducing a hyper-functional state that strengthens and prolongs direct cytotoxic responses; and immunogenic cell death (ICD) triggered by these effector cells broadens the tumor antigen repertoire, thereby enhancing cross-priming and diversifying host T cell responses.”
Comment 19) Minor comments Please revise for clarity/brevity:” …Of note, and relevant to a potential clinical setting, we have previously shown haploinsufficiency for the NR2F6 gene to be sufficient for the anti-tumor phenotype indicating that deletion of one allele will be sufficient (20).”
Response: Thank you for highlighting this point. We have revised the text for clarity and clinical relevance. Previous studies show that even partial reduction of NR2F6 function—such as in Nr2f6⁺/⁻ (heterozygous) mice—elicits the same antitumor phenotype as full knockout, confirming haploinsufficiency of the gene (Klepsch et al., Nat Commun, 2018, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-04004-2). This indicates that complete loss of NR2F6 activity is not required for therapeutic benefit, an encouraging finding for translational strategies where partial inhibition or monoallelic editing may be more achievable.
Manuscript addition (Introduction, lines 198–201): “Of note, and of potential clinical relevance, we have previously demonstrated that even partial loss of NR2F6, as seen in heterozygous knockout mice, is sufficient to elicit a robust anti-tumor phenotype (Klepsch et al., 2018b).”
Reviewer #3:
The manuscript presents highly interesting research on the advantages of Nr2f6 knockout in enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of CAR-T cell responses. To further strengthen this work, we would like to offer some additional considerations regarding the chosen methodology:
Response: We thank the reviewers for their positive feedback and appreciate their suggestions to further strengthen the manuscript.
Comment 1) Firstly, regarding Nr2f6, its function in T lymphocytes could be more clearly described in the introduction, even if briefly, to provide better context.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have added a concise description of NR2F6’s immunoregulatory function in T lymphocytes to the Introduction, for improved context.
Manuscript addition (Introduction, lines 140-160): “Here, we focus our investigation on the role of the orphan nuclear receptor NR2F6, a member of the COUP-TF of transcription factors, acting as an intracellular immune checkpoint, repressing NFAT- and AP-1–dependent cytokine transcription thresholds in effector T cells. It functions mechanistically as a ligand-independent transcriptional repressor that antagonizes the DNA binding of these transcription factors, thereby suppressing the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-2, IFNγ, TNFα, IL-17, and IL-21 (Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2008, Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2012, Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2015). The activity of NR2F6 is tightly controlled by PKC-mediated phosphorylation, which modulates chromatin association and transcriptional repression (Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2015). Through this molecular brake, NR2F6 maintains immune homeostasis and prevents excessive effector differentiation into highly activated T lymphocyte subsets (Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2008, Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2012, Hermann-Kleiter et al., 2015). Inhibition of NR2F6 enhances also NK cell effector function (Woelk et al., 2025) and improves pathogen clearance in a preclinical Listeria monocytogenes model (Jakic et al., 2021). Together with our previous studies identifying NR2F6 as an intracellular immune checkpoint in the effector T cell compartment (Klepsch et al., 2018b, Klepsch et al., 2018a), these findings establish NR2F6 as a promising therapeutic target for enhancing anti-tumor immunity. Moreover, NR2F6 expression in melanoma cells contributes to immune evasion and tumor progression, underscoring its dual role in the tumor microenvironment (Kim et al., 2023). These findings highlight the translational relevance of targeting NR2F6 in cancer immunotherapy and provide a rationale for exploring Nr2f6-deficient CAR-T cells in solid tumors.
Comment 2) Another aspect highlighted in some reports is the crucial role of CD4⁺ T cells in promoting and sustaining CAR-T cell responses in long-term responders. Carl June’s retrospective studies over a decade post treatment have demonstrated the persistence of predominantly CD4⁺ CAR-T cells. In this regard, we believe it would be valuable to evaluate the proposed therapeutic modification in this population, rather than focusing solely on CD8⁺ T cells. While the proposed mechanism of action—through antigen spreading—may be primarily driven by granzyme and perforin release from CD8⁺ T cells, the CD4⁺ subpopulation could also play a significant role in the overall response. Since recent published data show that long term persistence of CAR-T cells in the CD19+ tumor setting is found on CD4+ cells in patients and the authors show that the CD8+ CAR-T cell used do not last, it will be very important and informative to test solely transferring CD4+ CAR-T cells and also mixing CD4+ and CD8+ CAR-T cells to evaluate the impact on CAR-T cell persistence, antigen spreading and memory response formation.
Response: We thank the reviewers for emphasizing the importance of CD4⁺ CAR-T cells in sustaining long-term CAR-T persistence and function. Clinical and preclinical studies have shown that cytotoxic CD4⁺ CAR-T cells can exert direct antitumor activity via IFNγ–dependent mechanisms and play critical helper roles by shaping dendritic cells and CD8⁺ T cell activation. In response, we generated and tested Nr2f6-deficient CD4⁺ CAR-T cells, both alone and in combination with CD8⁺ CAR-T cells. Mixed or combined CD4⁺/CD8⁺ CAR-T infusions did not further improve tumor control compared to CD8⁺ CAR-T cells alone (see NEW Supplementary Fig.2H–K). We have clarified these results and their contextual relevance in the revised manuscript.
Manuscript addition (discussion, lines 516–518): “NR2F6 exerts immunoregulatory control in both CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells, but our data indicate that the enhanced antitumor activity is primarily mediated by CD8⁺ CAR-T cells (Suppl.Fig2H–K).”
Notably, CD4⁺Nr2f6-KO CAR-T cells alone delayed tumor progression relative to unmodified controls (Reviewer Figure 2), supporting a contributory, but secondary, role for this subset that warrants further mechanistic exploration in the future.
Reviewer Figure 2: Tumor growth kinetics following adoptive transfer of CD4⁺ or mixed CD4⁺/CD8⁺ Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells. Tumor-bearing mice received PBS (gray line), CD4⁺ Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells (solid green line), or mixed CD4⁺/CD8⁺ Nr2f6crispr-/- CAR-T cells (dashed green line) on day 5 after tumor inoculation. Tumor volume (mean ± SEM, n ≥ 5/group) was measured over time. CD4⁺ CAR-T cell treatment conferred superior tumor control compared to both the mixed-group and PBS, consistent with recent evidence that cytotoxic and helper CD4⁺ CAR-T cells can drive potent antitumor responses, sometimes independently or in concert with CD8⁺ CAR-T cells.
Comment 3) Additionally, although the proposed therapy is intended for solid tumors, hematological malignancies remain the only currently approved indication for CAR-T cell therapy and still require further optimization. In this context, we believe it would be important to evaluate the proposed approach either in this setting or in an alternative tumor model. Although the claim of the authors is based on the antigen spread phenomenon to explain the improved antitumor effect, testing the effect of Nr2f6 abrogation in a more classical setting such as a CD19+ leukemia or lymphoma could add potential clinical - validated implications to the manuscript.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment and agree that exploring NR2F6 abrogation in hematologic models, such as CD19⁺ leukemia or lymphoma, would provide additional translational perspective. In the present revision, we have expanded our study to include additional solid tumor models—B16-F10-hEGFR melanoma and MC38-hEGFR colon carcinoma (see NEW Supplementary Figure. 2A–G)—confirming that Nr2f6 knockout enhances CAR-T cell efficacy across distinct solid tumor types.
While evaluation in hematologic malignancies represents important future work, our current focus provides strong proof-of-concept in solid tumors, where therapeutic effectiveness of CAR-T cells remains most challenging. This focus aligns with recent findings showing that Nr2f6 inhibition improves CAR-T cell activation, proliferation, and memory across multiple solid tumor settings. We have clarified these points in the revised manuscript to emphasize both the immediate relevance to solid tumors and the broader translational potential of NR2F6 modulation.
Manuscript addition (Discussion, lines 514-516): “These results were comparable to those obtained with two independent CAR-T mouse models (B16-F10-hEGFR, MC38-hEGFR) (Suppl.Fig2A-G), which demonstrate the broad applicability of the obtained results.”

Response: We appreciate your participation in the Nature Communications peer review training and co-review initiative, and thank you for contributing to the constructive evaluation of our manuscript. Corresponding authors: Victoria Klepsch and Gottfried Baier
